To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
early-life antibiotic use was not associated with increased weight gain or obesity in children during the first years of life.

“in children, the rate of growth was similar in the first 8 y of life among children exposed to antibiotics in the 1st 6 mo of life vs unexposed children, and there were no clinically meaningful associations with the spectrum or number of courses of antibiotics.”
“early-life antibiotic use is not associated with the rate of growth during the first 3 years of life.”1
In summary, our research is concerned with
the association between early-life antibiotic exposures and the trajectory of weight gain in children.
the association of early-life antibiotic exposure with the rate of weight gain in all children.
the association between antibiotic use in early life and weight gain over the first 8.5 years.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no clinically meaningful association between early-life exposure to antibiotics and growth trajectories during childhood.

the use of antibiotics in infancy is not associated with an increase in the rate of growth during the first 3 years of life and, if any effect exists at all, it is small (150 g over 36 months) and clinically insignificant.1 1. Scott
the results of this study do not provide support for the hypothesis that early-life antibiotic use is associated with accelerated weight gain in the general population of children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we did not find a clinically meaningful increase in growth among children exposed to antibiotics during the first 6 or 24 months of life.
we observed no association between antibiotic exposures in the first 2 years of life and weight gain during the first 3 to 8 years of childhood.
the association between antibiotics and growth is weak and not clinically meaningful.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there was no clinically meaningful difference in growth trajectories between children who received early-life antibiotics and those who did not.
the use of antibiotics in the first months of life is not associated with clinically meaningful increases in growth over time.
